newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, retail sales, more selling?.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, retail sales, more selling?.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market gets two important pieces of economic data on Thursday but a key question is will the market continue its selloff?
"How the market trades overnight is really important," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston.
After moving lower overnight, the U.S. Treasury market sold off sharply in New York on Wednesday as a faltering U.S. dollar exacerbated worries that foreign investment in U.S. assets would slow.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond plunged nearly two full points on Wednesday, ending at 98-10/32. Its yield rose to 6.63 percent from 6.49 percent at Tuesday's close.
Analysts said there would be support for the market at 6.67 percent on the 30-year bond yield.

"That 6.67 percent has to hold," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi. "If it doesn't, there's going to be as much activity set off on the selling side as there was on the buying side when we came down through 6.75 percent in October."

Bonds rallied through the 6.75 percent level on the 30-year bond yield in October when the market learned that the third-quarter Employment Cost Index had reflected only a 0.6 percent increase in wages.
How bonds trade in the days ahead will depend greatly on the dollar, Alexy said.

"If (Japanese Ministry of Financial official Eisuke) Sakakibarato or one of his buddies makes a statement, watch the dollar and you'll see what happens to flows worldwide because everyone is long based on your dollar view," he said.
The dollar dropped sharply against most European currencies on Wednesday as players worried that the U.S. unit was stumbling on its record-breaking run.
Besides trying to swim through currents of nervousness and negative sentiment, the market must digest three pieces of significant economic data on Thursday.

The November Consumer Price Index (PPI) is expected to be up 0.3 percent, according to a Reuters poll. The core CPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, rose 0.2 percent, the economists estimated.
"We'll probably see airline fares rise," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "They often move in one direction for several months in a row."
And apparel prices could also be up. "I don't think retailers are discounting merchandise as much before the holiday season as they did last year," Moran said.
Still retail sales for November, of which chain and department store sales are only a portion, are expected to be up a very modest 0.3 percent after a 0.2 percent October gain.
Without autos, retail sales are expected to be up 0.3 percent from a 0.4 percent gain in October.

The Labor Department will also report new jobless figures for the latest week. Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that jobless claims rose to 341,000 in the week ended December 7 from 336,000 a week earlier.

John Williams, managing director and chief global markets economist at Bankers Trust, and James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities, expect claims to spike up to 350,000 due to a post-Thanksgiving Day holiday distortion.

"There's a little bit of a seasonal adjustment problem with this particular week," said Williams. "In general, claims are still running in the vicinity of 340,000 a week on a trend basis -- which is pretty low."
All the government data will be released at the same time -- 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1679
